headings.title: Introduction and Importance of the Foetal Skull in Obstetrics
headings.content: The foetal skull is one of the most critical anatomical structures that nursing students must master in obstetric nursing. Because the head is the largest and least compressible part of the term foetus, its passage through the maternal pelvis largely determines the progress and safety of labour. Understanding the anatomical layout of the foetal skull allows midwives and nurses to accurately assess the mechanism of labour, monitor foetal descent, and anticipate potential cephalopelvic disproportion—a condition where the foetal head is too large to fit through the maternal pelvis. Furthermore, clinical examinations such as abdominal palpation and digital vaginal examinations rely heavily on identifying skull landmarks to determine foetal presentation, position, and attitude. During labour, the bones of the skull can overlap, a process called moulding, which helps reduce the head dimensions to ease delivery. Any abnormal presentations or rigid structures can complicate delivery, making prompt identification vital for preventing maternal and neonatal morbidity. Therefore, a thorough knowledge of the foetal skull forms the foundational basis for safe intrapartum care in Nigerian hospitals and global obstetric practice.

headings.title: Bones of the Foetal Skull
headings.content: The foetal skull is structurally divided into the vault (cranium), the face, and the base. For obstetric nursing, the vault is of primary interest because it undergoes significant changes and adaptation during labour. The vault consists of several flat bones that are not yet fused together, separated instead by membranous spaces. These bones include the two frontal bones, two parietal bones, the occipital bone, and the temporal bones. The two frontal bones are still separate at birth and meet at the frontal suture. The two large parietal bones form the sides and roof of the skull, meeting at the sagittal suture. The occipital bone forms the back of the skull and the area surrounding the foramen magnum. The temporal bones lie at the sides below the parietals. Unlike adult skull bones which are firmly locked together by rigid sutures, the foetal cranial bones are thin, pliable, and loosely connected by connective tissue membranes. This unique composition allows the bones to shift and overlap when exposed to the strong compressive forces of the maternal uterine contractions, facilitating smooth engagement and descent through the birth canal without causing immediate trauma to the delicate underlying brain tissue.

headings.title: Sutures of the Foetal Skull
headings.content: Sutures are the membranous spaces that separate the individual bones of the foetal skull vault. They are crucial because they provide flexibility to the skull and allow for easy identification of the foetal head position during vaginal examinations. The main sutures include the sagittal suture, which runs between the two parietal bones from the anterior fontanelle to the posterior fontanelle. The frontal (metopic) suture runs down the middle of the forehead, separating the two un-fused frontal bones. The coronal suture lies between the frontal bones and the two parietal bones, running transversely across the head from left to right. Finally, the lambdoid suture separates the two parietal bones from the occipital bone at the back of the head, resembling the Greek letter lambda. During a digital vaginal examination in labour, feeling these sutures helps the nurse or midwife determine how the baby's head is rotated. If a suture feels unusually overlapping or widely separated, it can give vital clues about the progress of labour and whether moulding is occurring appropriately or if there is disproportion.

headings.title: Fontanelles and Their Clinical Significance
headings.content: Fontanelles are membrane-covered spaces where two or more sutures intersect, representing areas where ossification is incomplete at birth. The two most important fontanelles for clinical assessment are the anterior fontanelle (bregma) and the posterior fontanelle (lambda). The anterior fontanelle is diamond-shaped, relatively large, and bounded by the frontal and parietal bones; it typically closes between 12 to 18 months after birth. Clinically, a depressed anterior fontanelle may indicate dehydration, while a bulging fontanelle can signal increased intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus. The posterior fontanelle is triangular in shape and smaller, formed at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures; it usually closes by 6 to 8 weeks postpartum. In obstetric nursing, correctly identifying these two fontanelles during vaginal examinations is the gold standard for determining the exact position of the foetal head. For instance, feeling a diamond-shaped space points to the anterior position, while a small triangular space indicates the occiput is posterior or leading, helping guide clinical interventions.

headings.title: Regions and Landmarks of the Foetal Skull
headings.content: To accurately document foetal position and presentation, nursing and midwifery students must be familiar with specific regions and anatomical landmarks of the foetal skull. The vertex is the area bounded by the anterior fontanelle, the two parietal eminences, and the posterior fontanelle; it is the most common presenting part in normal vertex deliveries. The brow (synciput) extends from the anterior fontanelle and coronal suture to the root of the nose and supraorbital ridges. The face extends from the root of the nose and supraorbital ridges down to the junction of the chin and neck (mentum). The occiput is the area of the skull overlying the occipital bone, situated behind the posterior fontanelle, and serves as the universal landmark for designating foetal positions (e.g., Left Occipito-Anterior). Additionally, the parietal eminences are the widest points of the foetal skull vault, and their passage through the pelvic outlet is a major milestone in delivery. Recognizing these distinct surface landmarks during abdominal palpation (such as Leopold's maneuvers) and vaginal examinations enables nurses to evaluate labour progress and identify any malpresentations early.

headings.title: Diameters of the Foetal Skull
headings.content: The diameters of the foetal skull determine whether the head can successfully pass through the maternal pelvic planes. These imaginary lines are measured from specific points on the skull, and their lengths vary depending on the attitude (degree of flexion or extension) of the foetal head. The suboccipito-bregmatic diameter measures about 9.5 cm from the base of the occiput to the center of the anterior fontanelle; this is the smallest and most favourable anteroposterior diameter, occurring when the head is fully flexed. The suboccipito-frontalis diameter measures approximately 10.0 cm, extending from the occiput to the bridge of the nose with moderate flexion. The occipito-frontal diameter is about 11.5 cm, running from the bridge of the nose to the most prominent part of the occiput in an un-flexed (deflexed) head. The mento-vertical diameter is the longest anteroposterior measurement at roughly 13.5 cm, extending from the chin to the highest point of the vertex, seen in a brow presentation. Transverse diameters include the biparietal diameter (9.5 cm), which is the distance between the two parietal eminences, and the bitemporal diameter (8.2 cm), the distance between the widest parts of the temporal bones. Knowledge of these measurements is essential for anticipating cephalopelvic disproportion.

headings.title: Moulding of the Foetal Skull During Labour
headings.content: Moulding is the physiological overlapping of the cranial bones of the foetal skull that occurs as the head navigates the birth canal. Because the sutures and fontanelles are membranous and un-fused, the flat bones of the vault can slide over one another under the compressive forces of uterine contractions and pelvic resistance. This adaptive mechanism temporarily reduces the overall dimensions of the foetal head—particularly the transverse and anteroposterior diameters—making it easier for the foetus to pass through the pelvis. Moulding is graded clinically from 0 (no overlapping, sutures touch) to +++ (severe overlapping where bones are locked and cannot be easily separated), which nurses and midwives document during vaginal exams. While mild to moderate moulding is a normal, healthy sign of adaptation, excessive or rapid moulding can cause intracranial haemorrhage or tentorial tears due to extreme stress on bridging blood vessels. Postnatal nursing assessments should check for caput succedaneum or cephalhaematoma, which frequently accompany significant moulding. Understanding this process helps the nurse differentiate normal physiological adaptation from pathological cephalopelvic disproportion that requires immediate medical intervention.
